title: Clear the Marble Row
statement:
A row of coloured marbles is given as the string board. Each letter is one of R, Y, B, G, W. You also hold some marbles, given as the string hand.

On each turn you take one marble from your hand and insert it anywhere in the row: between two marbles or at either end. Then, while the row contains three or more marbles of the same colour in a row, that group vanishes and the two sides close up, which may form a new group that also vanishes.

Return the fewest marbles you need to insert to clear the whole row, or -1 if your hand cannot do it.

The starting row never contains three equal marbles in a row.

examples.why: Insert B into the BB pair. BBB vanishes, the row closes to GGG, and that vanishes too.
The lone B needs two more B marbles to vanish, and you hold only one.
Two R marbles clear the middle (WRRRW → WW), then one W finishes the row.

constraints: Only the letters R, Y, B, G, W
board has no three equal letters in a row
hints: The search space is small: at most 5 marbles to place and 17 positions each. Search it, but cache states you have already solved.
A state is the current row plus the multiset of marbles left in your hand. Sort the hand so equal hands share a cache entry.

Inserting a marble right after an equal marble is the same as inserting it before; skip duplicates. Do not limit yourself to placing a marble next to its own colour: dropping it between two equal marbles of another colour can set up a later chain.

explain.intuition:
The limits are tiny, which is the clue: this is an exhaustive search, made fast by remembering results. Write a function solve(row, hand) that returns the fewest marbles needed. It tries every marble colour in the hand at every position, collapses the row, and recurses. Cache the answer per (row, sorted hand).

The trap is pruning too hard. It feels obvious to only insert a marble next to one of its own colour, but sometimes the best move splits a pair of another colour, so that a later chain lines two halves back up. A safe pruning keeps two kinds of moves: next to the same colour, and between two equal marbles of a different colour. Other placements can be skipped; the first solution below tries every position and gives the same answers.
steps: Write collapse(row): repeatedly find a run of 3 or more equal letters and cut it out until none is left.
solve(row, hand): if row is empty return 0; if the hand is empty return infinity; check the cache.
For each distinct colour c in the hand and each position i: skip if row[i − 1] = c (same as an earlier position). Keep the move if row[i] = c, or if row[i − 1] = row[i] ≠ c.
Answer is 1 + solve(collapse(new row), hand without c), minimised over all kept moves. Cache and return it.
Return -1 if the result is infinity.
pitfalls: Only inserting next to the same colour. "BBRRBBRRBB" with "RR" needs an R dropped between two Bs first.
Removing only the first group and forgetting the chain reaction after the row closes up.
Caching on the hand in its original order, so "RB" and "BR" are solved twice.

complexity.time: Exponential in hand size, bounded by the cache: at most (states) · 5 · 17 moves

solutions.title: Breadth-first search, every position
solutions.idea: BFS over (row, sorted hand). Each level inserts one marble in every possible position. The first level that reaches an empty row is the answer.

solutions.title: Memoised search with safe pruning
solutions.idea: solve(row, hand) tries only useful moves: next to the same colour, or between two equal marbles of another colour. Results are cached by row and sorted hand.
solutions.time: Exponential in hand size, cut down by pruning and the cache

followups: The pruning never places a marble between two different colours that both differ from it. Argue why that is safe, or look for a row where it would fail.
How would you return the actual sequence of moves?
